write.desc: The global theorems for continuous functions, where compactness and connectedness (and behind them the completeness of R) turn continuity at each point into global facts: bounded, attained extrema, no skipped values, roots and fixed points. Each theorem is paired with counterexamples showing that every hypothesis is needed.

points.name: Continuous image of a compact set is compact
points.what: Prove that if K is compact and f is continuous on K then f(K) is compact, using sequential compactness: take a sequence in f(K), pull it back to K, extract a convergent subsequence, and push it forward by continuity.
outside: sequential compactness of a subset of R (every sequence has a subsequence converging in the set)

points.name: The same theorem with open covers
points.what: Give the second proof that continuous images of compact sets are compact, by pulling an open cover of f(K) back to an open cover of K and taking a finite subcover, and see why the two proofs agree on R.
outside: open-cover definition of compactness and Heine-Borel
topological form of continuity: preimages of open sets are open relative to the domain

points.name: The extreme value theorem
points.what: Prove that a continuous function on a nonempty compact set, in particular on [a,b], is bounded and attains a maximum and a minimum, and explain this as local continuity becoming global information through compactness.
outside: a nonempty compact subset of R contains its supremum and infimum (closed and bounded)

points.name: Why every hypothesis of the extreme value theorem is needed
points.what: Produce counterexamples when one hypothesis is dropped: x or 1/x on (0,1) (open interval), x on [0, infinity) (unbounded domain), a function on [0,1] with a jump or a pole (discontinuous), and 1/(x^2 - 2) on the rationals in [1,2] (domain in Q, not complete), and say which step of the proof breaks in each case.
outside: sqrt 2 is irrational and the rationals are dense in R

points.name: Continuous image of a connected set is connected
points.what: Prove that if E is connected and f is continuous on E then f(E) is connected, by showing that a separation of f(E) would pull back to a separation of E.
outside: definition of a connected set (cannot be split into two nonempty separated sets)

points.name: The intermediate value theorem via connectedness
points.what: State the intermediate value theorem (a continuous f on [a,b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b)) and derive it in a few lines from the connectedness of [a,b] and of its image.
outside: a subset of R is connected exactly when it is an interval

points.name: The intermediate value theorem directly: supremum and bisection
points.what: Prove the intermediate value theorem without topology, once by taking c = sup{x in [a,b] : f(x) < L} and ruling out f(c) < L and f(c) > L, and once by bisection with nested intervals, seeing exactly where completeness enters.
outside: axiom of completeness (least upper bound property)
epsilon-delta definition of continuity at a point (a continuous function keeps its strict sign near a point)

points.name: Why every hypothesis of the intermediate value theorem is needed
points.what: Show the theorem fails for a discontinuous function (a step function), on a domain that is not an interval, and for x^2 - 2 on the rationals in [0,2], and see that the converse fails: a function with the intermediate value property need not be continuous (sin(1/x) with value 0 at 0).
outside: the function sin(1/x) and its behaviour near 0

points.name: Continuous images of intervals are intervals
points.what: Prove that a continuous function maps any interval to an interval, and that it maps [a,b] onto exactly [m, M] where m and M are its minimum and maximum, combining the extreme and intermediate value theorems.
outside: definition of an interval as a set containing every point between any two of its points

points.name: Proving equations have solutions with the intermediate value theorem
points.what: Use sign changes to prove that equations such as x^2 = 2, x^n = a (a > 0) and cos x = x have solutions in a given interval, and use bisection to locate a root to any desired accuracy.

points.name: Every odd-degree polynomial has a real root
points.what: Prove that a real polynomial of odd degree takes both signs, because its leading term dominates for large |x|, and therefore has a real root; see why even degree gives no such guarantee (x^2 + 1).
outside: limits of polynomials at plus and minus infinity (the leading term dominates)

points.name: Fixed-point theorem on a closed interval
points.what: Prove that every continuous f: [a,b] -> [a,b] has a fixed point by applying the intermediate value theorem to g(x) = f(x) - x, and give counterexamples on (0,1), on [0, infinity) and for a discontinuous map.

points.name: Which hypothesis does each theorem need: compactness, connectedness, completeness
points.what: Sort the theorems of this topic by what they really use (compactness for boundedness and attained extrema, connectedness for intermediate values, completeness of R behind both) and, given a new statement, predict which hypothesis it needs and find a counterexample without it.
